extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners and communication/PR managers in organizations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on using radio and television for public relations: when to seek earned airtime, how to prepare PSAs and broadcast scripts, how to submit and technically format materials, how to time and evaluate broadcasts, and management considerations for choosing broadcast tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community bulletin-board eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Bulletin board announcements typically limited to nonprofit organizations or to nonprofit events sponsored by businesses; in largest markets limited to county-wide events and sprinkled randomly through programming rather than a fixed slot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A simple letter to the station manager often suffices to get an item read; it may be possible to telephone items to the promotion manager or news desk. Target nonprofit/local events and expect placement to be short and opportunistic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of press releases for radio
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases, especially when geared to radio’s special needs, can gain air time when you have a legitimate news story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor press releases to radio (concise, conversational, include audio-ready quotes). For staged events, ensure there's an obvious news hook so local news broadcasts will carry the item.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staged events as newsworthy publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Staged events (stunts, visual oddities) can create free news coverage when the publicity/press agent model is appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design stunts with a clear news angle and a connection to the promoted cause (example: a man dressed as a chicken promoting 'Eat More Chicken Week'). On slow news days local broadcasts may give several minutes to live onsite reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring and participation in talk shows
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk shows (call-in formats) can serve a PR function; organizations should assign well-informed members to monitor broadcasts and respond when relevant topics arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If conversation turns to issues within your purview, be ready with a standard line / brief statement and contact number; when topics are announced in advance, consider having organization members call in or appear as guest panelists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposing public-affairs programming
rubrics_metrics.description: Stations air public-affairs programs where newsmakers or representatives are interviewed; a call or letter proposing a program or segment usually will get a reply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect these programs to be aired late evening or early Sunday morning but still reach thousands. Propose segments that fit the station’s public-affairs formats and provide timely, newsworthy spokespeople.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pitching deejay chatter
rubrics_metrics.description: Disk jockeys often 'chat' with listeners and need new material; they may use intriguing tidbits while changing records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phone or drop a short letter with an intriguing tidbit. Keep pitches conversational and suitable to the deejay’s audience and format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal-time / right of reply considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Fairness Doctrine (personal-attack provision) stations must notify persons of the right of reply and furnish a copy of the original script; many stations broaden this to editorial-reply segments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equal-time and editorial-reply opportunities when criticized on air or when differing viewpoints need airing. The station will usually provide engineer/director assistance for replies and schedule them in similar time slots/formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized programming and underwriting
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities, trade organizations, and businesses can prepare programs or underwrite public radio/cultural programming in return for on-air credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer specialized content (e.g., expert interviews, career programs) or underwriting to gain broadcast exposure. Expect stations to provide credits at program openings/closings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four management considerations for using radio
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding whether to use radio consider: (1) Radio offers many formats (flexible medium); (2) Radio is primarily a local medium; (3) Radio has specialized stations with specialized audiences; (4) Nearly all publics use radio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate these generalizations into specific tactics—choose formats/stations that align with your audience, message, and desired interaction level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aligning broadcast format to PR model
rubrics_metrics.description: Different radio formats map to the four models of public relations: press agent/publicist, public information, two-way asymmetric, two-way symmetric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose formats consistent with your model: press agents use paid ads/deejay chatter; public-information specialists use news broadcasts/PSAs; two-way asymmetric uses paid announcements/PSAs/talk shows; two-way symmetric emphasizes dialogue (talk shows, call-in) to learn and negotiate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objectives for radio messages (agenda and retention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Objectives for radio should mirror those for print: get your organization on the radio agenda so people hear your message and retain it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select airing hours for target retention: drive time for professionals, daytime for homemakers, after-school for teens. If you can't predict acceptable air time or retention, choose another medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Realistic goals for paid radio advertisements
rubrics_metrics.description: Paid advertisements allow attempts to change attitudes and behavior, but such effects are difficult to attain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for communication, retention, and understanding rather than dramatic attitude change. Create persuasive announcements that listeners can remember and understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Program and station selection based on target publics
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio is most effective for public relations aimed at local publics; high-involvement publics often listen to selected stations at specific times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan carefully to communicate organizational concerns with active publics—choose the stations/times where your target publics are likely to listen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess time and monetary costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Radio is inexpensive if using press releases or getting representatives on talk shows, but producing PSAs or paid ads is costlier and time-consuming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Production costs include hiring talent, buying music rights, producing/distributing audio tapes, and buying time; use project planning tools (Gantt chart or network diagram) to coordinate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of radio impact
rubrics_metrics.description: To evaluate communication and retention objectives know if a station used your material, if anyone listened, and if listeners remember your message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use broadcast-monitoring services (air checks) in major markets; ask promotion directors for scripts/transcripts; PSAs customarily receive confirmation (a 'Paid' bill). Track responses with a unique phone/address or key phrase in radio spots and conduct follow-up phone surveys to measure impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing for the ear (radio spot preparation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing for audio requires economy and a conversational style unlike print; audio messages must be more economical and more conversational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use short, conversational sentences; avoid literal print translations. Ask people to read scripts aloud to check timing and clarity; be prepared to pare or add words after rehearsals and studio reads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time limits and timing metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Time is the critical limiting factor: thirty- and sixty-second formats are common; 60 seconds at moderate speed ≈ 140 words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate words per time (or 15 typed lines × 70 characters ≈ 1 minute), account for rapid/slow speech, and always rehearse read-aloud timing with actual voices to adjust copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sound elements and production expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Stations can add voices, 'real people' recordings, and have libraries of sound effects/music, but local stations won't produce highly slick, studio-level spots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select basic sound elements that stations can provide; for award-winning or high-production spots you’ll need special studios, directors, and engineers and then distribute recorded form to stations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create multiple length versions of spots
rubrics_metrics.description: Different versions should be written to fit standard time slots (e.g., 60, 30, 20, 10 seconds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the longer spot to introduce the campaign and shorter spots for repetition; shorter versions should retain main elements rather than introducing new information—flesh out ideas in longer versions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main reasons stations reject PSAs
rubrics_metrics.description: Stations must be selective; PSAs are commonly rejected for being too dry/dull, lacking a local angle, not blending with the station’s tone/format, or having poor technical quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make PSAs engaging, include local relevance, match station tone/format, and meet technical standards (see tape quality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical production standards for tape submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: Material submitted in tape form should be produced with studio-quality equipment on clean, quarter-inch magnetic recording tape; duplicates made on studio duplicators; frequent-use PSAs should be packaged on plastic cartridges ('carts').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only one copy is needed, cut the tape from the master and rewind on a small plastic reel. For multiple copies use a duplicator. Provide cart-format copies for frequent station use to increase chances of acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission routing and station contacts
rubrics_metrics.description: If unfamiliar with station management, direct material to the general manager; newsworthy items go to the news director; other formats to the program director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate contacts in news and programming departments. Always include the name, address, and phone number of someone in your organization on the covering letter, script, and tape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementing and promoting an audio 'Fone-Feed'
rubrics_metrics.description: An audio feed system lets stations call a number and receive one- or two-minute recorded material for automatic pickup (useful when PR departments supply quotes frequently).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promote the feed by phone-calling news directors, playing sample tapes, sending follow-up letters, and providing reminder cards/stickers near news-desk phones. Use the feed during periods of heavy media demand (conventions, tournaments, legislative sessions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing tape-loop content and staff responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The tape loop message should include an introduction and the voice 'actuality'; the sender must provide short daily items and designate staff to prepare tapes and maintain equipment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write the intro in all-capital format used by radio news personnel, list contact phone number, and indicate item lengths. Assign one staff member to prepare tapes, maintain equipment, and schedule feed availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flagging print releases for radio
rubrics_metrics.description: If the tape recorder carries voice actualities to 'illustrate' a print release, alert radio stations with a prominent note at the top of the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a special box/header such as: 'RADIO NEWS DIRECTORS, CALL FONE-FEED AT 999-9999 FOR SPOKEN VERSION OF MAJOR QUOTES IN STORY BELOW.'

rubrics_metrics.name: TV PSA content strategy and testing
rubrics_metrics.description: Television PSAs can be very effective but should be tested (e.g., focus groups); PSAs are most successful if they avoid preaching and stimulate new thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use focus groups to review storyboards/scripts and amend accordingly. Pair TV PSAs with talk shows and news programs to maximize impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Television production process and script format
rubrics_metrics.description: TV production is highly specialized: scripts should be split-page with visual descriptions on the left and dialogue/narration on the right; numerous story conferences and technical coordination are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure each word in a 30- or 60-second script conveys important information; work with technicians for sound, cameras, actors, props and estimate full project cost. Consider using outside film/video firms for professional production.
